comments.body:
## Root cause CONFIRMED by per-call measurement on i-00880b2c7f13527c5

Measured each suspect call individually on the production host (bounded, read-only, SSM).
Wall-clock per call:

| call | measured | bound in probe | completes? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `du -sx --block-size=1 /var/lib/docker` | **124.18s** (at a 130s probe bound) | `DOCKER_DU_TIMEOUT=120` | **NO** — always hits the cap |
| `du -sx --block-size=1 /var/lib/docker/overlay2` | same tree, second walk | `DOCKER_DU_TIMEOUT=120` | **NO** |
| `docker system df` | **25.01s** (at a 25s bound) | `DOCKER_DF_TIMEOUT=20` | **NO** |
| `journalctl -u rebar-autodeploy.service -o cat \| grep -c` | 8.19–14.11s | **unbounded** | yes |
| `journalctl CONTAINER_NAME=compose-review-bot-1 …` | 4.41s | **unbounded** | yes |
| `journalctl CONTAINER_NAME=compose-gerrit-1 …` | 8.93s | **unbounded** | yes |
| `du -sx /var/log/journal` | 0.01s | 60s | yes |
| `docker ps` / `docker stats --no-stream` | 0.04s / 2.62s | 15s | yes |
| gerrit/review-bot/MCP curl probes | 0.10s | `--max-time 10` | yes |

### The lead HELD, and it is worse than one `du`

`docker_du_bytes` is called **TWICE** (observability.sh:592-593) — once over `$DOCKER_ROOT` and
again over `$DOCKER_ROOT/overlay2`, which is essentially the same ~1.88M-file tree walked a
second time. Each is bounded at `DOCKER_DU_TIMEOUT=120` and each **always hits that bound**:

    592: docker_total_bytes="$(docker_du_bytes "$DOCKER_ROOT")"            -> 120s, returns nothing
    593: docker_overlay2_bytes="$(docker_du_bytes "$DOCKER_ROOT/overlay2")" -> 120s, returns nothing

**2 x 120s = 240s = TimeoutStartSec exactly.** The probe is SIGTERM-ed inside or immediately
after the second `du`. That is the whole 4-minute wall clock, and because `du` blocks on I/O
rather than computing, it contributes almost nothing to the ~35s CPU — which is the
wall-vs-CPU gap in the report.

Being *bounded* is not being *cheap*: the existing `timeout 120` guard converted an unbounded
hang into a **guaranteed 120s of burnt budget that returns no value**. Twice.

### Why it is this slow: the unit runs at idle I/O priority

`install-observability.sh` sets `IOSchedulingClass=idle` (and `Nice=10`) on the unit. On a host
with documented IOPS-saturation history (`smudgeless-friendless-longspur`), a 1.88M-file walk
at idle I/O priority is starved by design. So this is not fixable by raising the timeout or by
optimising computation — both were correctly ruled out in the report.

### Second contributor: 12 full-journal scans, all unbounded

The journal is **1.7 GB across 38 files**. The probe scans it end-to-end **12 times** in 5
distinct shapes — `publish_autodeploy_marker_delta` alone re-reads the identical
`journalctl -u rebar-autodeploy.service` stream **8 times** (lines 1310, 1312, 1318, 1322, 1330,
1343, 1348, 1350), plus one at 1301, plus voter/merge (2) and g2p (1). At the measured 8-14s per
autodeploy scan that is **~110s**, and it is the bulk of the ~35s CPU (journalctl decode + grep).

Neither contributor alone exceeds 240s. **Together they do**: 240 (du) + 20 (df) + ~110 (journal)
= **~370s of work in a 240s budget.**

### The cut point, and it matches the reported metric ages exactly

Metrics publish in file order. The kill lands at line ~593:

- line 97-237 — `gerrit_healthy`, `reviewbot_healthy`, `GerritReachable`, `mcp_healthy`,
  `disk_used_percent`, **`root_disk_used_percent` (192)**, `gate_scratch_mounted` — **all publish**.
- line 597+ — `docker_storage_bytes`, `journal_*`, `var_tmp_*`, `container_*`,
  **`mem_used_percent` (1020)**, `container_memory_rss_bytes`, `voter_errors`, `deploy_errors`,
  `g2p_dispatch_errors`, `mirror_out_of_sync` — **never reached**.

That is precisely the reported evidence: `root_disk_used_percent` fresh at 18:25Z,
`mem_used_percent` stale. The cut point moves with I/O load, which is why some late metrics
have occasional old datapoints rather than none.

### Confirmed still failing right now

Journal, this hour — every run killed at exactly 4min:

    18:20:49 Starting ... 18:24:49 killed 15/TERM, 'timeout', Consumed 39.687s CPU
    18:25:50 Starting ... 18:29:50 killed 15/TERM, 'timeout', Consumed 34.131s CPU
    18:31:13 Starting ... 18:35:13 killed 15/TERM, 'timeout', Consumed 39.518s CPU

### One correction to the report

`gerrit_healthy` is published EARLY (line 97) and does survive the kill, so "no datapoints at
all" is not explained by truncation. It is published **with an `InstanceId` dimension** while its
sibling `GerritReachable` is dimensionless; a query without that dimension returns nothing.
That is a query-side artifact, not a second defect in the probe.

comments.body:
## Correction to the previous comment — the journal scans are NOT a contributor

I checked the deployed script against `origin/main` before building on the journal figure, and my
"12 unbounded full-journal scans" was measured against the shape the ticket description cites, not
against the code actually running. `md5sum /usr/local/bin/rebar-observability.sh` matches current
main: the marker counters were already converted to **cursor-anchored, bounded** reads by bug
`1205-63b2-2c01-4e7f` (`journal_marker_delta` uses `--after-cursor` under
`bounded "$JOURNAL_SCAN_TIMEOUT"`, default 10s). There are 7 `journal_marker_delta` call sites,
each reading only entries since its own cursor. On a healthy box that is a few entries, not 1.7 GB.

The 8-14s per-scan numbers I measured are what a *full* scan costs; the probe no longer does one.
**Withdraw that contributor.** The remaining cause stands on its own and is cleaner for it.

## The cause, restated on the corrected evidence: two walks of one tree

    592: docker_total_bytes="$(docker_du_bytes "$DOCKER_ROOT")"             # du -sx /var/lib/docker
    593: docker_overlay2_bytes="$(docker_du_bytes "$DOCKER_ROOT/overlay2")" # du -sx the same tree again

`overlay2` is essentially all of `/var/lib/docker`, so this walks ~1.88M files **twice per run**,
each bounded at `DOCKER_DU_TIMEOUT=120`.

**2 x 120 = 240s = `TimeoutStartSec=240` exactly.** Under I/O contention both walks hit their cap
and the SIGTERM lands with zero budget left for everything after line 593 — which is every metric
the report lists as missing. This is not an approximate fit; it is the timeout to the second.

And the second walk buys nothing. The code's own comment says `docker_overlay2_bytes` is
"deliberately no longer [participating] in the arithmetic" — it survives only as a breadcrumb in
one `logger` line. **120s of the 240s budget, in the worst case, is spent on a log message.**

### Frequency, refined

24h on the host: **55 timeout kills against 197 completed runs** (~22%). The kills are *clustered*
— five consecutive between 18:19 and 18:36 — because they happen when the host is under I/O load.
Which is the operator's point: the probe goes blind exactly when the box is in trouble.

Corroborating this, `du` sometimes completes: `docker /var/lib/docker bytes=` breadcrumbs land at
17:48, 17:58, 18:03, 18:09, 18:42. So the walk ranges from tens of seconds to over the 120s cap,
and even a "good" run spends ~50% of the probe's entire budget in these two calls.

### The unit makes it worse by design

`install-observability.sh` sets `IOSchedulingClass=idle` and `Nice=10`. A 1.88M-file walk at idle
I/O priority on an IOPS-saturated host is starved deliberately. Correct for a background probe;
fatal when that probe's tail carries the metrics an operator reads under load.

## Fix, three parts

1. **One walk, not two.** `du -x --max-depth=1 $DOCKER_ROOT` yields the grand total *and* the
   `overlay2` subtotal from a single traversal. Halves the worst case, 240s -> 120s, and removes
   the walk that existed only for a log line.
2. **Deadline-clamped expensive calls with a reserved tail budget.** The script records its start
   and clamps each expensive call to `min(own timeout, deadline - now - TAIL_RESERVE)`. The `du`
   can then never consume the budget the later sections need.
3. **Truncation publishes itself** — `probe_ok` + `probe_elapsed_seconds` on completion, and an
   `ExecStopPost` hook that publishes `probe_truncated=1` when systemd reports a non-`success`
   result. systemd runs `ExecStopPost` after a timeout SIGTERM, so a killed run emits its own
   death certificate.

On acceptance criterion 4 (positional dependence): choosing **the reserve, not reordering**.
Reordering only moves which metric starves; a guaranteed tail reserve means no metric can be
starved by an earlier section overrunning, whatever the order.

Impact update, measured 18:49 UTC — the alarm surface has degraded further, and it is now overwhelmingly false.

**19 alarms in ALARM.** The metrics behind them:

    data_disk_debris_bytes            journal_cap_in_effect            review_bot_merge_change_errors
    disk_used_percent                 journal_used_percent             review_interrupts_bound_exceeded
    docker_buildkit_cache_used_percent  mcp_mem_abort                  review_interrupts_signal_unavailable
    docker_storage_used_percent       mcp_retire_cap                   var_tmp_cleanup_active
    docker_unaccounted_bytes          mirror_out_of_sync               var_tmp_used_percent
    g2p_dispatch_errors               replication_errors               voter_errors
    gate_scratch_mounted

**Newest datapoint and value for a representative sample:**

    root_disk_used_percent   18:44Z (5 min ago)   = 73
    mem_used_percent         18:39Z (10 min ago)  = 65
    voter_errors             18:39Z (10 min ago)  = 0
    replication_errors       18:39Z (10 min ago)  = 0
    journal_used_percent     18:39Z (10 min ago)  = 57
    gerrit_healthy           NO DATA in 4 hours

So the metrics are publishing, recently, with **healthy values** — zero errors, journal at 57%, memory at 65%, root at 73%. Only two of the nineteen correspond to a real condition: `gate_scratch_mounted` (0, the unmounted volume — `dcc3`) and `var_tmp_cleanup_active` (0, awaiting the `rootflags=pquota` reboot). Both are known and operator-pending.

**Roughly 17 of 19 alarms are reporting a condition that is not true.** Earlier today the same count was 4 of 6. The ratio is getting worse as the probe is killed earlier in its run.

**A second observation that supports the memory-pressure link, and is worth someone testing properly.** `mem_used_percent` stalled completely between 17:40Z and 18:39Z — 49 minutes with no datapoint. It resumed after I restarted the MCP container at ~18:32, which took host memory from 83% used / 990 MB available to 4,314 MB available. That is consistent with the probe getting further through its run when the host is not thrashing, i.e. memory pressure aggravates the I/O stall rather than causing it. One observation, one intervention — suggestive, not established, and the per-section timing this ticket asks for would settle it.

**Why the ratio matters more than the count.** An operator facing 19 alarms of which 17 are false cannot triage by reading the alarm names; they have to go to the datapoints for every one, which is what the alarm surface exists to spare them. I did exactly that three times today and twice nearly drew the wrong conclusion — once treating a cluster of five as a submit-triggered incident, once reading a firing BuildKit alarm as evidence of a real overshoot when it had been red on missing data since the previous evening.

comments.body:
## Margin measurement, and a third finding the measurement forced

Re-measured on i-00880b2c7f13527c5 at 19:03 UTC, load average 3.45 — representative of the
condition that produces the kills.

    95.01s rc=124  timeout 95  du -x --block-size=1 --max-depth=1 /var/lib/docker
    95.01s rc=124  timeout 95  du -x --block-size=1 --max-depth=1 /var/lib/docker
   125.03s rc=124  timeout 125 du -sx --block-size=1 /var/lib/docker
   125.04s rc=124  timeout 125 du -sx --block-size=1 /var/lib/docker/overlay2

**The walk does not complete at any bound.** Not at 95s, not at 125s, twice each. Yet it
completes in well under a minute when the cache is warm (breadcrumbs at 17:48, 17:58, 18:03,
18:09, 18:42). The reading is **bimodal — fast, or unobtainable** — which retires the idea that
a bigger ceiling buys a reading. It buys only a longer stall. `DOCKER_DU_TIMEOUT` therefore
goes to **60**, capturing the fast mode and failing fast in the stalled one; §2e already says a
measurement that could not be taken publishes as silence, and `docker_du_seconds` now says why.

### Third finding: the ceilings were never composed, and the real worst case was ~495s

Timing the tail exposed that `du -sx /var/tmp` **also** exhausts its bound (15.06s at a 15s
probe), and that led me to inventory every wall-clock bound in the script rather than only the
one I came for:

| bound | ceiling |
|---|---|
| 2 x docker root `du` | 120 + 120 |
| `docker system df` | 20 |
| `du /var/log/journal` | 60 |
| `du /var/tmp` | 60 |
| per-entry `du -sk` loop | 10 x N |
| `docker ps` + `docker stats` | 15 + 15 |
| 7 cursor-anchored journal reads | 7 x 10 |
| `git ls-remote` | 15 |

**Over 495s of ceilings inside a 240s timeout.** Every one carries a comment justifying itself
against that timeout; the journal section literally reasons "12 scans x 10 s = 120 s < the
240 s TimeoutStartSec" while the docker section was separately entitled to 240s of the same
budget. Each ceiling is individually correct and the set is individually wrong. **Nobody was
adding them up** — that is the defect class, and the double `du` was only the instance that
happened to hit first.

So the fix is not "make the `du` cheaper" but "hold the budget in one place":

- `probe_budget_left` = `PROBE_DEADLINE_SEC - elapsed - PROBE_TAIL_RESERVE_SEC` (240 - 80).
- `clamped <ceiling> <cmd>` grants `min(ceiling, budget_left)` and every wall-clock-bounded call
  in the script now goes through it — all 13 of them.
- A `clamped` call starting at t cannot end after `deadline - reserve`, and **no sequence of
  them can either**. The clamped portion of a run is bounded at **160s by construction**, not by
  estimate.

### Margin

- **Guaranteed: 80s** (240 - 160), and it is structural — it does not depend on how slow the
  disk gets, because a stalled call is granted less, not more.
- **Measured typical: ~105s elapsed, so ~135s margin.** From the host, at load average 3.45:
  docker walk <=60, ledger 15, `/var/log/journal` du 0.01s, `/var/tmp` du ~15, `docker ps` 0.03s,
  `docker stats` 3.22s, `free` 0.02s, three health curls 0.69s total, `git ls-remote` 0.25s,
  seven journal reads 0.49-1.69s each.
- Floor of 1s rather than 0 on an exhausted budget, deliberately: a clamped call must still RUN
  and fail, because "could not be measured" is publishable and being SIGKILLed is not.

### Answering criterion 4 — reserve, not reordering

Reordering only changes *which* metric starves. A reserve no earlier section can spend means
none can. Pinned by a defect-seeded test: the `du` stub is driven 3s past a 2s budget and the
assertion is that `mem_used_percent` — the metric that went blind for 49 minutes, and which
sits ~400 lines after the walk — still publishes, and that `probe_ok` still follows it.

### Criterion 3 — truncation is now a signal

`probe_ok` (once, last), `probe_elapsed_seconds`, and `probe_truncated` from an `ExecStopPost`
hook that systemd runs even after a timeout SIGTERM. Two alarms in `monitoring_9313.tf`:
`probe_truncated` (notBreaching — ExecStopPost cannot run if the unit never ran) and the
missing-data arm of `probe_ok` (breaching — that is the "no runs at all" case).

### Tests

12 new tests in `tests/scripts/test_observability_timeout_9313.py`. Verified RED against
`origin/main`: **10 of the 12 fail** on the unfixed script, including
`expected exactly one docker-root walk per run, got ['-sx --block-size=1 /var/lib/docker',
'-sx --block-size=1 /var/lib/docker/overlay2']`. The 12th is a ratchet asserting no wall-clock
bound bypasses `clamped`, so the composition hole cannot be quietly reopened.

comments.author: Rebar Bot
comments.body:
## Meeting the raised evidentiary bar — hypothesis, in-situ proof, discriminating result, revert condition, mutation check

The dispatch lead (`du` in `docker_du_bytes`) was treated as a lead. Answering the five points
in order, and one of them changed my conclusion.

### 1. Falsifiable hypothesis, and what would disprove it

**H:** the wall clock between the unit's `Starting` and its SIGTERM is consumed inside the
docker-storage section, specifically in the two `docker_du_bytes` calls at observability.sh:592-593.

**Disproof, stated before the test:** the probe emits `logger -t rebar-health` breadcrumbs at
fixed line positions. If H holds, a killed run must show breadcrumbs up to *and including* the
gate-scratch line (:214, the last one before the docker section), then **nothing**, then the
kill — and must **never** show the `docker /var/lib/docker bytes=` line (:598), which is only
emitted when the first walk returned a value. **Any** of these would disprove H:

- a killed run showing the `:598` docker breadcrumb (walk finished, time went later);
- a killed run showing the `buildkit cache` (:619) or `journal ceiling` (:697) breadcrumbs;
- a killed run whose silence begins *before* the gate-scratch breadcrumb (a network probe);
- the gap being materially smaller than the run.

### 2. In-situ proof, not isolated re-timing

My first measurement re-ran the suspect commands standalone. That is inference from
plausibility, and the objection is right. The probe already instruments itself — timestamped
breadcrumbs at known line offsets — so I interleaved `journalctl -t rebar-health` with the unit
lifecycle over 90 minutes. **Ten consecutive killed runs, one fingerprint:**

    19:29:49  UNIT   Starting rebar-observability.service...
    19:29:58  CRUMB  gate scratch /var/lib/rebar/gate-scratch mounted=0     <- :214
              (231 seconds of complete silence)
    19:33:49  UNIT   Main process exited, code=killed, status=15/TERM
    19:33:49  UNIT   Failed with result 'timeout'.  Consumed 41.981s CPU time.

Identical at 18:47:55, 18:52:56, 18:57:56, 19:02:56, 19:08:58, 19:14:58, 19:19:57, 19:25:02,
19:35:58. Prologue **7-13 s**; then **~231 s / 96% of the run inside one section**; and the
`:598` breadcrumb **never appears in any killed run**, so the FIRST walk does not complete
either. 9 + 120 + 120 = 249 against a SIGTERM at 240 — the kill lands mid-second-walk, which is
what the arithmetic predicts.

Contrast, the one completed run in the window (18:43): breadcrumbs flow continuously —
`var_tmp` 18:43:40, `container writable` :41, `memory` :45, four container rows :48-:51 —
and it consumed **1 min 5.4 s** CPU against the killed runs' 31-46 s.

### 3. Discriminating — the same data refutes the alternatives

This is not a test that merely fits H; each rival predicts a *different* breadcrumb pattern and
none of them occurs:

| rival hypothesis | its prediction | observed |
|---|---|---|
| journal marker counters | crumbs through `:697`/`:793`, then silence | never reached |
| `docker system df` | `:598` present (it precedes the ledger read) | **never present** |
| a network probe | silence *before* the gate-scratch crumb | crumb always lands, at 7-13 s |
| general host slowness | prologue also stretched | prologue is 7-13 s |

And on "a fix that lets a stalled probe stall longer": **this change does not raise the
timeout.** `TimeoutStartSec` stays 240. The timeout is not the defect and moving it would only
move the kill point, exactly as the report says.

### 4. NEGATIVE RESULT — part of this is a capacity finding, and I am saying so

Removing the second walk is **not sufficient**, and I would have shipped believing it was if I
had stopped at the isolated timings. A **single** walk does not complete at a 95 s bound or at a
125 s bound (twice each, load average 3.45), and the in-situ data agrees: walk #1 never
finished in any killed run. So:

**The Docker root cannot be walked inside this probe's budget under load. That is a capacity
finding, not a defect.** ~1.88M files, at `IOSchedulingClass=idle`, on a host with IOPS
saturation history.

The right response to a capacity limit is to stop spending unbounded budget against it, not to
enlarge the budget. So `DOCKER_DU_TIMEOUT` goes **down** (120 -> 60): the reading is bimodal —
cache-warm and fast, or unobtainable — and a 120 s attempt that fails costs a minute more than a
60 s attempt that fails, for no reading either way. When it is unobtainable the §2e rule
applies: publish silence, and let `docker_du_seconds` say why.

**The genuine defect is the composition**, which the capacity limit merely exposed first: the
script held over **495 s** of independently-defensible ceilings inside a 240 s timeout, each
with a comment justifying itself against that timeout, and nothing adding them up. `clamped`
fixes that, and it is the load-bearing part of the change — not the halved walk.

### 5. RED for the right reason, then perturbation

**RED:** 10 of 12 tests fail against `origin/main`, and on the right assertion —
`expected exactly one docker-root walk per run, got ['-sx --block-size=1 /var/lib/docker',
'-sx --block-size=1 /var/lib/docker/overlay2']`.

**Perturbation found a real hole before it found teeth.** The portability `timeout` stub this
suite inherits is `shift; exec "$@"` — it discards the duration — so replacing every `clamped`
with `bounded` left all twelve tests green. The mechanism could have been deleted silently. Two
tests added that measure the **grant** rather than the behaviour: exhausted budget must hand the
walk `1`, full budget must hand it `60`. Seven mutations, all killed:

| mutation | killed by |
|---|---|
| M1 reintroduce the second walk | `walked_exactly_once` |
| M2 clamp ignores the budget | `clamp_hands_an_exhausted_budget` (granted 60s) |
| M3 delete the completion heartbeat | 3 tests |
| M4 `--report-exit` always reports success | `killed_run_publishes_probe_truncated` |
| M5 deadline drifts from `TimeoutStartSec` | `probe_deadline_matches_the_unit_timeout` |
| M6 revert `--max-depth=1` to `-s` | `walked_exactly_once` (shape arm) |
| M7 one raw `bounded` reintroduced | ratchet + exhausted-budget test |

### Revert condition — what would mean I was wrong

Revert if, after deploy, **any** of these holds:

1. `probe_truncated` still reports 1, or `probe_ok` is still absent, on more than an isolated
   run. The composition invariant is structural, so this would mean the stall is somewhere I
   have not clamped — i.e. H was incomplete.
2. `probe_elapsed_seconds` sits above ~160 s. That is the clamped-portion bound; exceeding it
   means unclamped work I did not account for dominates.
3. `mem_used_percent` still shows multi-interval gaps while `probe_ok` reads 1. That would
   falsify the positional-independence claim directly — the tail would be starving for a reason
   other than the budget.
4. The four gap-firing alarms (criterion 6) do not clear on unchanged thresholds. The
   report's own standard, and the honest test of whether this diagnosis was complete.

Expected and NOT a revert trigger: `docker_storage_bytes` / `docker_unaccounted_bytes` going
intermittently silent under load, with `docker_du_seconds` at 60. That is the capacity finding
surfacing correctly rather than a regression, and it is strictly better than today, where the
same walk fails AND destroys the rest of the run. Sizing the Docker root within a probe budget
is separate work and should get its own ticket.

## In-situ attribution — the raw evidence

Recording the primary data behind the proof, since the conclusion rests on it.

Interleaved `journalctl -t rebar-health` (the probe's own timestamped breadcrumbs, at known
line offsets) with the unit lifecycle, 90-minute window, production Gerrit host. Ten
consecutive killed runs; here are three verbatim:

    18:47:48  UNIT   Starting rebar-observability.service...
    18:47:55  CRUMB  gate scratch /var/lib/rebar/gate-scratch mounted=0
    18:51:49  UNIT   Main process exited, code=killed, status=15/TERM
    18:51:49  UNIT   Failed with result 'timeout'.  Consumed 45.944s CPU time.

    19:14:49  UNIT   Starting rebar-observability.service...
    19:14:58  CRUMB  gate scratch /var/lib/rebar/gate-scratch mounted=0
    19:18:49  UNIT   Main process exited, code=killed, status=15/TERM
    19:18:49  UNIT   Failed with result 'timeout'.  Consumed 43.266s CPU time.

    19:29:49  UNIT   Starting rebar-observability.service...
    19:29:58  CRUMB  gate scratch /var/lib/rebar/gate-scratch mounted=0
    19:33:49  UNIT   Main process exited, code=killed, status=15/TERM
    19:33:49  UNIT   Failed with result 'timeout'.  Consumed 41.981s CPU time.

Also at 18:52:56, 18:57:56, 19:02:56, 19:08:58, 19:19:57, 19:25:02, 19:35:58 — same shape every
time. Prologue 7-13 s. Then **231 seconds in which the probe emits nothing at all**, and it
emits nothing because it is inside the docker `du`.

The completed run at 18:43, for contrast — every breadcrumb after the docker section arrives,
seconds apart:

    18:43:21  CRUMB  var_tmp /var/tmp budget=unsetB cleanup_active=0 hard_quota=0
    18:43:40  CRUMB  var_tmp /var/tmp bytes=3841892352
    18:43:41  CRUMB  container writable share=unsetB reaper_active=0 quota_enforceable=0
    18:43:45  CRUMB  memory available_percent=34 used_percent=65
    18:43:48  CRUMB  container compose-review-bot-1 service=review-bot memory_rss_bytes=169659597
    18:43:49  CRUMB  container rebar-mcp-... service=mcp memory_rss_bytes=1723355628
    18:43:50  CRUMB  container compose-opcert-1 service=opcert memory_rss_bytes=38702940
    18:43:51  CRUMB  container compose-gerrit-1 service=gerrit memory_rss_bytes=787585434
    18:44:12  UNIT   Consumed 1min 5.416s CPU time.

Two things fall out that I had not measured before.

**The `mem_used_percent` gap is now explained end to end.** It is emitted at 18:43:45 in the run
that completes and in none of the ten that do not — a metric published or not published purely
by whether the `du` in front of it returned. That is the operator-facing consequence in the
report, reproduced from the host's own log.

**A complete run costs ~65 s of CPU; a killed one 31-46 s.** So the killed runs are not doing
*more* work and failing to finish — they are doing *less*, and blocking. The report's
wall-versus-CPU inference is confirmed from a second direction.

comments.body:
## Independent CloudWatch sweep corroborates the mechanism — plus one thing it does NOT explain

A parallel agent's presence sweep (period=300, 96 buckets/metric, 8 h) landed while this was in
review. It is an independent instrument — CloudWatch presence, not the host journal — and it
measures the same thing my breadcrumb trace does, from the other end:

    lines 112-213  (head)         93% present   max gap 10 min
    line  601  docker_storage     70%                   35 min
    lines 622/640 buildkit        31%                   60 min
    line  798  var_tmp_used        0%                    -
    lines 1193-1301 counters   48-53%                 60-70 min
    lines 1463/1511 g2p/mirror    43%                   85 min

**Monotone decline in presence with line number.** That is the positional mechanism measured
from the metric side, and it agrees with the journal trace metric-for-metric: 93% at the head,
falling off sharply at the docker section (line 601 is the first metric after the walk), and
`var_tmp_used_percent` at **0%** — a metric that has never once been reached.

Two consequences worth recording.

**The consumer dependency is satisfied by this change.** A downstream agent has documented an
operator workaround — "a reading-alarm firing on absence means the probe could not measure
this" — because with the probe dead before section 2, `disk_used_percent` is absent for reasons
having nothing to do with the volume, and the alarm cannot tell "the disk is full" from "the
probe never measured it". That information is genuinely not in the metric today. `probe_ok`,
`probe_elapsed_seconds` and `probe_truncated` are in change 2684 and turn that inference into a
fact. The consumer's guidance can become a lookup instead of a heuristic once it lands.

**NEGATIVE RESULT — the 25-minute HEAD gap is not explained by this root cause, and I am not
claiming it.** The same sweep reports the head-of-script max gap widening from 10 to 25 minutes,
and four false alarms at 20:47Z on missing data while the conditions were verified healthy. The
head runs *before* the docker walk: my breadcrumb trace shows the prologue completing in 7-13
seconds on every one of ten killed runs, and the gate-scratch breadcrumb landing every time. So
a 25-minute head gap is roughly four to five missed runs at the observed 5-6 minute cadence, and
**my root cause cannot produce it.** Something else is dropping whole runs or failing the
`aws put-metric-data` calls at the head. That is a second defect and deserves its own ticket
rather than being folded in here on a plausible story — which is the mistake this whole
investigation exists to correct.

One checkable prediction rather than a claim: each killed run currently *occupies* 240 s of a
~300 s timer period, leaving ~60 s of slack, so any additional delay pushes a run into the next
period. After this change a run takes ~105 s, restoring ~195 s of slack. **If the head gap
narrows after deploy, cadence pressure was a contributing factor; if it does not, the second
defect is independent and the follow-up ticket is required.** Either outcome is informative,
and `probe_elapsed_seconds` is what will settle it — today the run duration is visible only in
`systemctl`, never in a metric, which is precisely the gap this change closes.

Filed as **change 2684** — https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/c/rebar/+/2684

comments.body:
## Is the composition invariant guarded? It is now — and the first version of the guard had a hole

Stating this as a decision rather than leaving it implicit: **the invariant is BUILD-ENFORCED,
not a convention.** `test_every_wall_clock_bound_goes_through_clamped` is a source scan over
`observability.sh` that fails if `timeout` or `bounded` appears in command position anywhere
outside the two lines that form the door (`bounded`'s own definition, and `clamped`'s single
delegation to it).

A source scan rather than a runtime check, deliberately: the grant tests observe only the calls
a fixture actually reaches, so a bare `timeout` on a branch behind a host condition the stubs
do not produce would pass them. The scan sees every call site whether or not any test executes
it.

### The guard did not initially hold, and the check is why I know

Asked whether it was guarded, I checked rather than asserted, and the honest first answer was
**partly**. The original scan matched only `timeout "$VAR"` and `bounded <digits>`. So I
reintroduced the exact shape named as the risk — a bare `timeout 15 docker ps`, which is the
form two of the original nine ceilings actually had — and:

- the **source scan passed**. It did not see it.
- the **runtime grant test failed**, catching it by accident of coverage.

Caught by the weaker of the two mechanisms, for a reason that would not generalise. Had that
call sat on a branch the fixture does not reach, both would have passed and the composition bug
would have been back with no signal. The scan now matches either helper in command position
with any argument, and I re-ran the mutations rather than trusting the regex:

| reintroduced shape | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `timeout 15 docker ps` (bare literal) | **MISSED** | caught |
| `timeout "$VAR_TMP_DU_TIMEOUT" du -sx` | caught | caught |
| `bounded 15 git ls-remote` | caught | caught |
| `bounded "$JOURNAL_DU_TIMEOUT" du -sx` | caught | caught |
| a brand-new `timeout 30 …` at line start | **MISSED** | caught |
| a brand-new `timeout 30 …` after a pipe | **MISSED** | caught |

Three of six shapes were invisible to the first version. The scan over-matches and then
subtracts the two sanctioned lines by exact text, so a new spelling of the door fails loudly
instead of quietly widening it.

The rationale is now also stated at the definition site in `observability.sh`, so the next
person adding a bounded call reads it before the test tells them.

## The accepted degradation is filed

`docker_storage_bytes` / `docker_unaccounted_bytes` going intermittently silent under load is a
**chosen trade**, and an undocumented regression the moment it lives only in a handoff message.
Filed as **`utopic-frenzied-albino`** (`5993-4cf7-0de9-4f72`, p2), linked `discovered_from` this
ticket, carrying the 95 s and 125 s negative results, why 60 s is still correct given the
bimodal distribution, what is lost (`docker_unaccounted_bytes` is the incident metric), four
options with none pre-selected, and the alarm question a deliberate non-measurement raises
against `treat_missing_data = "breaching"`.

The distinguishing signal is recorded there and in the script: a gap with `docker_du_seconds`
≈ 60 and `probe_ok` = 1 is the trade working as designed; a gap with `probe_ok` absent or
`probe_truncated` = 1 belongs to this ticket's revert conditions.

## Plan-review gate returned BLOCK, and all three findings were correct

Ran the gate to earn the attestation the `bugfix-size-attestation` finding on change 2684 requires.
Verdict **BLOCK**, 3 blocking findings. I am recording them because they are not gate noise — two
of them are the exact corrections my own investigation had already produced, and the gate caught
that I had left them in COMMENTS while the DESCRIPTION still asserted the original, wrong story.

That is a fair hit. A comment thread six entries deep does not correct a plan; the plan is what the
next reader acts on.

### Finding 1 + 2 (E4, G1G2) — the metric-ordering claim contradicted the script

> `gerrit_healthy` is published near the TOP (line 97) while `mem_used_percent` is published near
> the END (line 1020). Under the plan's own 'position decides survival' mechanism, an early metric
> should SURVIVE a mid-run kill, so 'no datapoints at all' cannot be explained by lateness.

Correct, and I reported exactly this in my first comment — `gerrit_healthy`'s absence is a
dimension artifact (`InstanceId` on one side, dimensionless `GerritReachable` on the other), not
truncation. The description still listed it as "later still", which is the single most load-bearing
sentence in the causal story and it was false. **Fixed in the description**, and the ordering
bullets now cite metrics whose positions I verified: `root_disk_used_percent` (192),
`docker_storage_bytes` (601), `mem_used_percent` (1020), `var_tmp_used_percent` (798, 0% present),
`mirror_out_of_sync`/`g2p_dispatch_errors` (1463/1511).

### Finding 3 (G6) — the LEAD framed an unbounded call that does not exist

> Every du/df in observability.sh is already `timeout`-wrapped, so the overrun is the SUM of
> bounded calls (two 120s docker du calls alone reach the 240s TimeoutStartSec) — reframe AC1 to
> measure cumulative section time against a global budget rather than to find a single blocking
> call.

This is the composition finding, arrived at independently by the gate reading the same code. The
description told an implementer to hunt one unbounded blocker; they would have found nine bounded
ones and no culprit. **AC1 is reframed** to require cumulative attribution against a global budget
and to account for the existing bounds explicitly.

### Advisories, both adopted

- **AC4 deferred the remediation mechanism** ("either ordered so none can starve, or each publishes
  independently — state which"). Now committed: **a reserved tail budget no earlier section can
  spend**, with the reason stated (reordering only moves which metric starves).
- **A global wall-clock budget was not considered as an alternative.** It is now AC2 — the sum of
  bounds must be *provably* below `TimeoutStartSec`, with the guaranteed margin stated. That is
  what `clamped` does in change 2684.

Also adopted from the dropped set: a **back-out path** AC, since this feeds live dead-man alarms.

### Net

The gate blocked on the plan disagreeing with the code — which is precisely what it is for, and
the disagreement was real. The implementation in 2684 already matches the corrected plan; what was
stale was the plan itself. Description rewritten (6,842 chars, under the 8,000 admission cap;
`file_impact` unchanged at the same 5 paths, so nothing widened). Re-running the gate.

comments.body:
## Second gate run: BLOCK on one finding, and it is the sharpest one yet

Verdict BLOCK, **1 blocking finding at validity 1.0**, down from 3. The three earlier findings are
resolved. This one is better than the ones it replaced:

> AC5's committed mechanism ('a reserved tail budget that no earlier section can spend') is named
> but its ENFORCEMENT in a non-preemptive, sequential, single-process shell script is unspecified.
> In straight-line bash, if an earlier timeout-wrapped section blocks for its full ceiling, the
> tail section never starts — **no budget 'reservation' can preempt an already-running blocked
> call.**

That is correct, and it is a real gap in the plan rather than in the code. "A reserved tail budget"
describes a *guarantee*, and in a single-process shell script there is no mechanism that could
deliver it as stated: once `timeout 120 du` is blocked, nothing reclaims that budget for a later
section. A reader given only the plan would be entitled to conclude the mechanism is impossible —
and on the plan's own wording they would be right.

The implementation was never doing the impossible thing. It does the **inverse**, which is
enforceable: rather than reserving budget for the tail, it *shrinks every call's ceiling as the
deadline approaches*, so no call can run into the reserved window in the first place. The gate's
own suggested fix describes it almost exactly:

> at start-of-run the probe computes an absolute deadline = start + (TimeoutStartSec -
> TAIL_RESERVE); every section, before beginning, compares `now` to (deadline) and if it cannot
> finish within remaining budget it skips…

which is `PROBE_STARTED_AT` + `probe_budget_left` + `clamped` in change 2684. So this is a **plan
defect, not an implementation defect** — the description asserted an outcome and omitted the
mechanism that makes it achievable, and the gate refused to certify a guarantee it could not see a
path to. That is the correct call.

**AC5 rewritten** to state the enforcement path concretely: the absolute deadline, the
`min(own ceiling, budget_left)` grant, the derivation that a call starting at any t cannot end
after `deadline - reserve` and no sequence of them can either, and the 1s floor with its reason
("could not be measured" is publishable; being SIGKILLed is not). Split into separate criteria per
the P6 advisory, each with how it is verified — notably that the GRANT is asserted, not merely
that the run completed.

### The admission cap is a real trap

The rewritten description came out at **8,596 chars against the 8,000 admission cap** — which would
have blocked the very re-review the gate demands as the remedy. Trimmed narrative (not evidence:
every measurement, line number and timestamp is retained) to **7,995**, applied with no
`description_warning`. Worth stating plainly for the next person: the remedy for a BLOCK is
usually to say MORE, and the cap pushes the other way, so budget for it.

Fourth run started.

## `Verified -1` on patchset 2 — a real failure, and a guard from a parallel workstream

Not environmental, and not rechecked. Three cells (py3.11/3.12/3.13) failed identically:

    FAILED tests/unit/test_alarm_window_tuning.py::test_breaching_alarms_require_every_period_in_the_window
    monitoring_9313.tf:observability_probe_truncated      period=300 evaluation_periods=3 datapoints_to_alarm=2 breaching
    monitoring_9313.tf:observability_probe_not_completing period=300 evaluation_periods=3 datapoints_to_alarm=2 breaching

Ticket `a9d1-c7f3-cfd9-44ff` (`illbred-sour-alpaca`) merged while this was in review and landed
that invariant plus `infra/runbooks/alarm-window-tuning.md`. **I1:** a `breaching` alarm must have
`datapoints_to_alarm == evaluation_periods`, because under `M < N` missing buckets can OUT-VOTE a
real datapoint — a gap pages on its own, and a slow publisher holds the alarm in ALARM
*unclearably*. Measured: 10.5 hours stuck on `rebar-docker-buildkit-cache-high`, and four
simultaneous false alarms at 20:47Z against verified-healthy infrastructure.

My alarms were authored at `M=2 of N=3` before that test existed. The guard caught a real
violation in my change. That is the second time in this ticket a structural check has caught
something no behavioural test could see, and I note that the alarm workstream and I arrived at the
same conclusion from opposite ends — they measured the gaps my probe was producing, I measured the
truncation producing them. The runbook names `probe_ok`/`probe_truncated` as the canonical
dead-publisher and truncation signals once this lands.

### The fix, and the branch I did not take

Both alarms move to **`M = N = 6` over `period=300`** — a 1800s window, Profile A.

**Keeping `breaching`.** I1 offers `notBreaching` as an alternative when an INTERMITTENT breach is
the real condition, and there is a sanctioned opt-out marker for it. I did not take it, because
the reasoning already recorded on this ticket settles the branch the other way: `ExecStopPost`
fires on EVERY stop and a successful one publishes `probe_truncated = 0`, so a healthy period is a
published 0 and silence means a dead publisher. That is precisely the precondition `breaching`
exists for. Taking the opt-out would undo the correction `make verify` forced on me earlier.

**30 minutes, not the 900s I2 floor** — and for a reason specific to these two metrics rather than
by copying the profile. `probe_ok` is emitted LAST in the script, so it gaps whenever a whole run
is dropped, and the 25-minute head-of-script gap measured at 20:47Z is a **separate, still-open
defect** (`fragile-matronal-vole` / `a7bd-0cee-404f-4c06`) that drops runs outright. A 15-minute
window here would page on that other bug. Revisit when `a7bd` closes and the cadence is
re-measured — the measurement should set it, not the aspiration.

**The cost, stated rather than hidden:** at `M = N` a single truncated run no longer pages. What
pages is 30 minutes of continuous truncation — which is the condition actually observed (55 kills
against 197 runs in 24h, clustered), not a lone blip. A one-off truncation is still a published
datapoint and still visible on the metric.

Rebased onto current `origin/main` (now containing `a9d1` and `1bffbd58`). The failing test and its
sibling suite pass locally (29), my own tests pass (43), lint clean. **Patchset 3 pushed to change
2684**; the stale `Verified -1` was removed by the push.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## Truncation is a GRADIENT ordered by script position — measured, with the cut point quantified

Measured 2026-09-06 02:33 UTC over a 3-hour window, `rebar/host`, 300s period. Rather than asking
"is metric X missing", I sampled across the probe's script order and looked at counts and staleness
together. The result is not a binary alive/dead — it is a clean monotonic falloff:

| metric | datapoints in 3h | last published |
|---|---|---|
| `mcp_healthy` | 24 | 25 min ago |
| `gate_scratch_mounted` | 24 | 25 min ago |
| `mem_available_percent` | 22 | 25 min ago |
| `docker_unaccounted_bytes` | **17** | **55 min ago** |
| `docker_buildkit_cache_percent` | **0** | never in window |
| `container_writable_used_percent` | **0** | never in window |
| `var_tmp_used_percent` | **0** | never in window |

A full window is 36 buckets. Metrics near the head reach 24; the middle degrades to 22 then 17 with
growing staleness; the tail reaches zero. That ordering is the signature of a run that is cut off
part-way through, with the cut point varying per invocation — not of individual collectors failing
independently, which would produce no such ordering.

### The deployed fix DID help — and is not sufficient

`mem_available_percent` now publishes 22 samples with a 25-minute age. Earlier measurement on this
same metric found it published **ZERO for five consecutive hours** (12:00-16:00 PDT) while
`mcp_healthy` published 7-12/hour in the same runs. So `aaa31f11f3bc` ("Compose the observability
probe's time budget", change 2684) moved the cut point materially later and recovered a metric that
was entirely dark. It did not eliminate truncation: three metrics still never publish at all.

This is worth stating precisely because it changes the fix's disposition. The composed time budget
was the right change and it demonstrably worked; what remains is that the total work still exceeds
the budget, so the tail is still amputated. A further increase in the budget alone would move the
cut point again without removing the failure mode — the collectors need to be individually bounded
and independently emitted, so that a slow collector costs only its own metric rather than every
metric after it.

### This explains an apparent host regression that is NOT one

The host alarm count rose from 6 to 8 in the last hour, adding `rebar-docker-buildkit-cache-high`
and `rebar-docker-unaccounted-bytes`. **Neither is a breach.** Their last known values were healthy
and comfortably inside their thresholds:

```
docker_buildkit_cache_percent   threshold > 85.0      last values: 52, 56, 56, 56
docker_unaccounted_bytes        threshold > 2.147e9   last values: 1.73e9, 1.58e9, 1.73e9, 1.88e9
```

Both fired because their metric went silent, not because it went high. So the observable "the host
got worse" is false; what actually happened is "the probe published less", and two more metrics
crossed from the publishing side of the cut to the silent side.

That is a dangerous property in itself and worth calling out: **as the probe truncates further, the
alarm count RISES, which reads as host degradation.** An operator responding to this page would
start investigating docker disk usage, which is fine. The failure mode is the inverse case — if a
metric goes silent while its underlying condition is genuinely breaching, the dead-man fires with
the same shape, and the two are indistinguishable from the alarm alone. Every one of these must be
adjudicated on datapoints, never on alarm state or StateReason.

### Not to be "fixed" by touching the alarms

For the avoidance of doubt: the remedy is the publisher, not the alarms. Do not widen these windows,
raise the thresholds, or set them to notBreaching. A dead-man alarm firing because its publisher
died is the alarm working correctly.

compiled_state.description:
## The defect

`rebar-observability.service` does not publish sparsely. It is **killed part-way through most runs
under load**, and every metric published after the kill point never appears at all.

From the host journal, 2026-09-05:

    18:25:50  Starting rebar-observability.service - rebar health + disk observability probe...
    18:29:50  rebar-observability.service: Main process exited, code=killed, status=15/TERM
    18:29:50  rebar-observability.service: Failed with result 'timeout'.
    18:29:50  rebar-observability.service: Consumed 34.131s CPU time.

`TimeoutStartUSec = 4min`; the run spans **exactly** 18:25:50 -> 18:29:50. Not finishing late —
SIGTERM-ed on the timeout. Frequency: **55 timeout kills against
197 completed runs in 24h**, clustered under I/O load — i.e. when an operator most needs it.

## The decisive measurement: 4 minutes wall-clock, ~35 seconds CPU

Consumed CPU: **34.131s** and **39.687s** against 4 minutes of wall time. The probe is ~3.4 minutes
**BLOCKED**, not computing. Raising the timeout only moves the kill point; a faster script does
nothing.

## The mechanism is CUMULATIVE, not a single unbounded call

An early framing named `docker_du_bytes`'s `du -sx` an unbounded multi-minute blocking call.
**That is wrong and is corrected here.** Every expensive call is ALREADY `timeout`-wrapped: `DOCKER_DU_TIMEOUT=120`, `DOCKER_DF_TIMEOUT=20`,
`JOURNAL_DU_TIMEOUT=60`, `VAR_TMP_DU_TIMEOUT=60`, `JOURNAL_SCAN_TIMEOUT=10`, and literal `timeout 15`
on the docker/`git ls-remote` calls. There is no unbounded blocker to find.

The defect is that **nothing composes those bounds**. `docker_du_bytes` is called TWICE
(observability.sh:592-593, over `$DOCKER_ROOT` and again over `$DOCKER_ROOT/overlay2` — essentially
the same ~1.88M-file tree), and 2 x 120 = **240s = `TimeoutStartSec` exactly**, before the journal,
var_tmp, container, memory or counter sections run at all. Summing every ceiling in the file gives
**over 495s inside a 240s timeout**. Each carries a comment justifying itself against that
timeout; the journal section reasons "12 scans x 10s = 120s < 240s" while the docker section is
separately entitled to 240s of the same budget. Every ceiling is individually correct and the set
is individually wrong. So the investigation must measure **cumulative section time**.

## Why this is the root cause of several open tickets

Metrics publish sequentially, so a metric's POSITION decides whether it survives the kill:

- `root_disk_used_percent` (line 192, early) — fresh, 10 points in 60 min. Healthy.
- `docker_storage_bytes` (line 601, the first metric AFTER the walk) — 70% present, 35 min max gap.
- `mem_used_percent` (line 1020, late) — newest datapoint 17:40Z, nothing for ~49 minutes.
- `var_tmp_used_percent` (line 798) — **0% present**; never once reached.
- `mirror_out_of_sync` / `g2p_dispatch_errors` (lines 1463/1511, last) — 43% present, 85 min gaps.

One mechanism explains three recorded mysteries: `illbred-sour-alpaca` (alarms firing on healthy
operation — the empty buckets are the section never running), `enviable-beloved-buffalo` ("three
metrics published nothing for 7+ days" — never reached), and `herbal-garish-monkey`'s dead-man
design being fed by a publisher that silently truncates itself.

**A correction:** an earlier version of this ticket listed `gerrit_healthy` as "later still — no
datapoints at all". That is wrong. `gerrit_healthy` is published at **line 97, the EARLIEST of the
three**, and it survives the kill. Its apparent absence is a query-side artifact: it carries an
`InstanceId` dimension while its sibling `GerritReachable` is dimensionless, and CloudWatch keys a
metric by namespace+name+dimensions. It is NOT evidence of truncation and must not be used as such.

Measured consequence: of six alarms in ALARM at 17:09 UTC, only **two** were genuine.
`docker_unaccounted_bytes` read 1.87 GB against a 2 GiB threshold; BuildKit read 10% against 85.

## Operator consequence, observed first-hand

A session used `mem_used_percent` to decide when to restart a leaking MCP process. It went blind
for 49 minutes while the leak continued. **A probe that truncates itself removes exactly the
signals an operator reaches for under pressure**, because pressure is what makes it slow enough to
be killed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Cumulative attribution by measurement: per-section elapsed time summed against the 240s
      budget, naming which sections consume it, accounting for the existing per-call `timeout`
      bounds rather than seeking one unbounded call.
- [ ] **The reserve is enforced by an absolute deadline, not by reservation.** Stating this is
      required because a "reserved budget" is not achievable by preemption in a straight-line,
      single-process shell script: once an earlier `timeout`-wrapped call is blocked it runs to its
      own ceiling and nothing interrupts it, so a later section can still be starved however much
      is nominally reserved. The enforceable form is the inverse — shrink each call's ceiling as
      the deadline approaches:
      - record `PROBE_STARTED_AT` at start of run, and define
        `budget_left = PROBE_DEADLINE_SEC - elapsed - PROBE_TAIL_RESERVE_SEC`;
      - grant every wall-clock-bounded call `min(its own ceiling, budget_left)` instead of its own
        ceiling, so a call beginning at any time t cannot END after `deadline - reserve`, and no
        sequence of such calls can either;
      - floor the grant at 1s, not 0, so an over-budget call still RUNS and fails fast — "could
        not be measured" is publishable, being SIGKILLed is not.
- [ ] Verified by asserting the GRANT each call receives — exhausted budget gives the floor, full
      budget the call's own ceiling — not merely that the run completed.
- [ ] Every bounded call routes through that one grant helper, enforced by a check that fails if a
      call site bypasses it. Verified by reintroducing a bypassing call.
- [ ] The clamped portion of a run is bounded by construction at
      `PROBE_DEADLINE_SEC - PROBE_TAIL_RESERVE_SEC`. State that bound and the margin it leaves.
- [ ] `PROBE_DEADLINE_SEC` equals the unit's `TimeoutStartSec`, enforced by a check, so the probe
      cannot budget against a deadline systemd does not apply.
- [ ] The probe completes within its timeout under representative load over consecutive runs.
- [ ] A truncated run cannot be silent: a killed or early-exiting run publishes that fact, so "the
      section never ran" is distinguishable from "the value is missing". Today they are identical.
- [ ] The truncation signal needs no network call, so it publishes during the stall it reports.
- [ ] Defect-seeded: drive a call past the whole budget; the late metrics still publish and the
      completion signal still fires.
- [ ] Re-measure the alarm surface: alarms firing on gaps clear without threshold changes. If not,
      the diagnosis is incomplete.
- [ ] Back-out path: this feeds live dead-man alarms, so the prior probe revision must be
      revertible via the normal deploy path.
- [ ] Portability: host shell + systemd + local validation; no single-CI-provider dependence.

## Testing

1. RED first: show a run exceeding 4 minutes with ~35s CPU, killed at the boundary.
2. Attribute the wall clock in situ — the probe's own timestamped `logger -t rebar-health`
   breadcrumbs sit at known line offsets, so interleaving them with the unit lifecycle brackets
   each section without adding instrumentation.
3. Confirm which metrics fall after the kill point and that they match the observed absences.
4. After the fix, verify late-section metrics publish on consecutive runs under induced I/O load.

## Provenance

Found 2026-09-05 while investigating why `mem_used_percent` had stopped publishing. The gaps were
repeatedly mis-attributed to "cadence jitter" and "sparse publishing" because a truncated run and a
slow publisher are indistinguishable from the metric side. The journal settles it.
